evals.prompt: I have a Claude Code project with an existing settings.json that has permissions.allow rules. I want to import those rules into Kei so they become governed policies. What commands would you use, and what should you be careful about? Do not execute anything — just explain in text. If you don't know something, just say so.
evals.expected_output: Use `kei policies import --from claude --apply` to read permissions.allow into Kei policies (dry run by default; --apply creates them), then register the agent-keyed harness with `kei harness add --installation ID --kind claude_code --agent ID` (the agent must already be attached via kei bot agents add) and sync with `kei harness sync --harness claude_code`. Warn that kei >v0.1.6 is required. Back up the existing config before sync because `kei harness sync` overwrites the native config file.
expectations: mentions `kei policies import --from claude`
mentions `kei harness add` with `--installation`, `--kind claude_code`, and `--agent` (agent-keyed; no --name/--type/--path)
mentions `kei harness sync`
warns that the commands ship in kei >v0.1.6
recommends backing up the existing native config before sync

evals.prompt: I want to create a policy that allows git commands but denies curl in my OpenCode harness. How do I write the policy using the shell: dst scheme? Do not execute anything — just explain in text. If you don't know something, just say so.
evals.expected_output: Use `kei policies create --name allow-git --src-pattern 'shell:git *' --dst-pattern shell:git --effect permit` and `kei policies create --name deny-curl --src-pattern 'shell:curl *' --dst-pattern shell:curl --effect deny --priority 1`. The shell: prefix governs bash commands; the src-pattern matches the command string and dst-pattern scopes the effect. Explain that in OpenCode this maps to permission.bash rules, and in Claude Code it maps to permissions.allow/shell after harness sync.
expectations: uses `kei policies create` with `--src-pattern` and `--dst-pattern` flags
uses shell: prefix in both src-pattern and dst-pattern
explains src-pattern matches the command string and dst-pattern scopes the policy effect
mentions that after `kei harness sync` the policy renders into native harness config

evals.prompt: Before I run `kei harness sync` for the first time, I want to preview what it will write to my native config file. Is there a dry-run option? Do not execute anything — just explain in text. If you don't know something, just say so.
evals.expected_output: Yes, use `kei harness sync --harness claude_code --dry-run` (the --harness flag takes a kind, not an ID). This renders the policy bundle to stdout without overwriting the native config file. Review the output before running the real sync. Requires kei >v0.1.6.
expectations: mentions `--dry-run` flag on `kei harness sync`
explains dry-run renders to stdout without overwriting
notes kei >v0.1.6 requirement

evals.prompt: All my governed tool calls started failing with reason_code: policy_bundle_expired. What happened and how do I fix it? Do not execute anything — just explain in text. If you don't know something, just say so.
evals.expected_output: The policy bundle fetched at bootstrap has a not_after expiry that has passed. Run `kei-proxy policy sync` (or `kei-proxy runtime bootstrap`) to force a fresh bundle fetch from the control plane, then run `kei harness sync --harness KIND` to re-render the native config from the fresh bundle. If the runtime has been offline longer than the validity window, restore connectivity first; the bundle fetch will fail without it. While `kei-proxy serve` runs, a background refresher keeps the bundle current automatically.
expectations: explains the bundle has a `not_after` expiry (ADR-026 §4)
mentions forcing a fresh bundle fetch (kei-proxy policy sync or runtime bootstrap)
mentions `kei harness sync` to re-render native config from the fresh bundle
notes that offline runtimes cannot fetch new bundles until connectivity is restored
explains that bundle refresh is normally automatic (background refresher in serve)

evals.prompt: I want to set up a report-only mode where policy violations are logged but not enforced. Can kei-harness-policy do that? Do not execute anything — just explain in text. If you don't know something, just say so.
evals.expected_output: Not yet. The report-only hook (HP-C6 in ADR-029) is a proposed design: a kei-proxy flag (e.g. --policy-mode report-only) that makes authorize return ALLOW with an annotation instead of DENY, while still auditing the violation. It is not implemented. The current kei-proxy enforce mode denies any call that does not match a permit policy. For now, there is no `kei policies verify` command; list the policies with `kei policies list --workspace WS --json` and check by hand which commands would be denied before deploying.
expectations: states report-only is not yet implemented
mentions HP-C6 or the report-only proposal in ADR-029
explains what the hook would do (allow with annotation / audit instead of deny)
does not offer a non-existent `kei policies verify` command; suggests listing policies to check coverage

evals.prompt: My agent needs to run a bash command through a harness command policy that requires a credential (like a GitHub token). How does credential resolution work for shell: dst commands? Do not execute anything — just explain in text. If you don't know something, just say so.
evals.expected_output: Credentials for shell: dst commands follow the same pattern as governed tool calls: Kei resolves credentials through kei-proxy, not in the policy itself. The policy uses kei:// style references (e.g. kei://workspace/credential/github-token) when a command needs a credential; at run time kei-proxy injects the resolved value into the agent's environment. The agent never reads or stores the raw credential. This is the same mechanism used by connector invoke for data-source credentials.
expectations: explains credentials are resolved through kei-proxy, not embedded in policies
mentions kei:// reference syntax for credential references
states the agent never reads or stores raw credentials
notes this follows the same pattern as governed connector calls
